message.content: Lions (family Felidae) and zebras (family Equidae) diverge deep in the mammalian tree. Their most recent common ancestor is a member of the clade **Laurasiatheria**, which includes all modern carnivorans, perissodactyls, cetartiodactyls, and a few other groups. That ancestor was a small, insect‑eating mammal that lived roughly **100–120 million years ago** during the early Cretaceous. In other words, the common ancestor of lions and zebras is a Laurasiatherian mammal that predates the split between the lineages that led to modern carnivorans (cats, dogs, bears, etc.) and perissodactyls (horses, rhinos, tapirs).
message.reasoning:
The user asks: "What is the common ancestor of lion and zebra?" We need to answer. This is a biology question. The common ancestor of lions (Panthera leo) and zebras (Equus quagga) would be a common ancestor in the mammalian tree. They belong to different families: lions are Felidae (cat family), zebras are Equidae (horse family). Both are part of the order Carnivora? Wait, zebras are not carnivores; they are in the order Perissodactyla (odd-toed ungulates). Lions are in Carnivora. So their common ancestor would be at the level of mammals, perhaps the last common ancestor of all placental mammals or maybe the last common ancestor of all mammals. But we can say: The common ancestor of lions and zebras would be a common ancestor of all mammals, likely a small, insectivorous mammal that lived around 200 million years ago. But we can also mention that they diverged from a common ancestor of the clade that includes both the perissodactyls and carnivorans. That common ancestor would be a member of the clade Laurasiatheria. Actually, lions and zebras are both Laurasiatherian mammals. The last common ancestor of all Laurasiatherians would be the common ancestor of the group that includes carnivorans, perissodactyls, cetartiodactyls, etc. That ancestor would have lived about 100-120 million years ago. But we can keep it simple: The common ancestor of lions and zebras is a common ancestor of all mammals, likely a small, insect-eating mammal that lived around 200 million years ago.
